meta.description: Satchel Paige said it. Quote Investigator traces it to an Associated Press column of 2 October 1959 — and finds older echoes.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't pray when it rains if you don't pray when the sun shines'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Paige. Traced to a 1959 AP column — with a metaphor that reaches back to an 1890 Kansas newspaper.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator traced the line to a column by Associated Press writer Hal Boyle, published 2 October 1959, which quotes Paige directly. QI’s conclusion is unambiguous: Paige should receive credit for the statement.

source.heading: A 1959 Associated Press column
source.excerpt: Never let your head hang down. Never give up and sit down and grieve. Find another way. And don’t pray when it rains if you don’t pray when the sun shines.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ reproduces the passage from a 1959 Hal Boyle column for the Associated Press and concludes that “Satchel Paige should receive credit for the statement in the 1959 citation.”

QI’s earliest citation is dated 2 October 1959 in the Moberly Monitor-Index of Missouri. Wikiquote ↗ instead cites the New York Post of 4 October 1959 — two days later. QI separately lists a 1992 quotation dictionary that carries the same New York Post citation.

QI records three earlier appearances of the same metaphor that are not credited to Paige: an 1890 piece in a Ravanna, Kansas newspaper, a 1917 Billy Sunday sermon printed in the Atlanta Constitution, and a 1920 newspaper filler item. Paige gets credit for the saying, not for inventing the image — Quote Investigator ↗.
A 1971 edition of Bartlett’s Unfamiliar Quotations carried the quotation but misspelled his name as “Sachel” — Quote Investigator ↗.
source.excerptNote: The famous sentence is the last of four. Quote Investigator reproduces the passage from Hal Boyle’s 1959 column; the run-up is what gives the closing line its shrug.

author.name: Satchel Paige
author.heading: About Satchel Paige
author.metaLine: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
author.bio: Leroy Robert “Satchel” Paige pitched across five decades, most of them in the Negro leagues, where he became one of the most famous and successful players in the game without being allowed into the major leagues. He finally reached them in 1948, at an age nobody could agree on, and in 1971 became the first player inducted into the Hall of Fame from the Negro leagues. He talked the way he pitched — unhurried, and with something on it.

misattribution.heading: Whose line is it, exactly?
misattribution.intro: Paige is the right speaker. The complication is that the image was already in circulation when he used it.

items.why: A piece titled “Pray While the Sun Shines” ran in the Ravanna Chieftain in 1890, telling a story about a child taught to pray in fair weather as well as foul — Quote Investigator ↗.
The evangelist preached in 1917 that “They don’t pray when the sun shines, they wait until the storm rages,” as printed in the Atlanta Constitution — Quote Investigator ↗.
A 1992 quotation dictionary QI cites carries that New York Post date. QI’s own earliest citation is two days earlier, in an Associated Press column — Quote Investigator ↗.
Bartlett’s Unfamiliar Quotations (1971) printed the quotation under a misspelling of his name — Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗: Paige should receive credit for the statement, while using a figurative frame that reaches back to a nineteenth-century story and a Billy Sunday sermon.

context.heading: Four sentences on how to keep going
lead: By 1959 Paige was in his fifties and had spent most of his career in the Negro leagues, barnstorming past the age at which most pitchers stop. The line arrives at the end of a short run of advice about not giving up, which is the register it belongs to: not piety, but stubbornness.
It works as an argument about fair-weather anything. Turn up only when you need something and you have not really turned up.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI traces the quotation to a 2 October 1959 Hal Boyle Associated Press column in the Moberly Monitor-Index and concludes Paige should receive credit.
QI documents 1890, 1917 and 1920 precursors of the metaphor not credited to Paige, and a 1971 Bartlett’s misspelling of his name.
Wikiquote cites the New York Post of 4 October 1959 for this quotation.
Paige lived 1906-1982, pitched in the Negro leagues and MLB, and entered the Hall of Fame.
